title: Día de los Muertos
hookLine: in Mexico families welcome the dead with marigolds, photos and favorite foods

cards: A small table against the living room wall is filling up. A framed photo of an abuelo in his good hat. Candles.
A plate of his favorite food, still warm. A bottle of the soda he liked. Sweet bread.
Paper cut into lace in bright colors. And everywhere, orange: marigolds, heaped in pots and scattered in a path of petals toward the door. Nobody is setting this table for the living.
It's for the people who have died, and the family expects them. This is the ofrenda, the offering, for Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead.

teach.b: In the way families describe it, the dead return for these days to be with the people who love them. So the ofrenda isn't a memorial in the usual sense.
It's hospitality: you put out a guest's favorite food because a guest is coming.
The marigolds' color and scent, families say, help guide the dead home, which is why the petals make a path. The photo says who is expected.
The water, the food, the candles say welcome, you must be tired from the journey.
Families also go to the graves, clean and decorate them with flowers and candles, and stay, sometimes through the night, eating, talking, playing music. It can look like a party.
For the families who keep it this way, it is one, a loving one. It comes at the start of November, alongside the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls, which you met earlier in this block.

In Mexico, as the story is often told, those days meet older Indigenous ways of honoring the dead, and families keep it in their own ways. It isn't Halloween. The painted and sugar skulls are smiling, not scary.
Look back at the week: graves that remind us, going home, knowing how to die, a skull that wanted to stay dead, life first, a broom on a hillside, and now a table set for guests.
Different peoples, different beliefs, and the same quiet refusal to let the dead become strangers.

how: For Día de los Muertos, families in Mexico and in Mexican communities elsewhere build ofrendas at home with photos, marigolds, candles and the dead's favorite foods, and families visit and decorate graves; customs vary by region and family.

games.why: the ofrenda is hospitality: you set out what the guest loved, because, as families describe it, the guest is coming.

practice: Find a photo of someone who has died, on paper or on your phone, and set it where you can see it, with a flower, a leaf, or a cup of something they liked beside it.
Then sit with them a while: if they were coming to visit, what would you want to tell them about your year?
